events.title: Earliest Historical Records
events.description: Chinese texts recorded Singapore region as 'Pu-luo-chung,' a trading post at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Early Singapore played a role in East-West trade.

events.title: Temasek Period
events.description: Singapore was known as 'Temasek' (meaning 'Sea Town'), serving as a trading outpost for the Srivijaya and Majapahit empires.

events.title: Singapura Legend
events.description: According to the Malay Annals, Srivijayan prince Sang Nila Utama saw a mysterious animal (legendarily a lion) and named the place 'Singapura' (Lion City).

events.title: Attacked by Siam and Majapahit
events.description: Singapura Kingdom was destroyed by attacks from Siam to the north and Majapahit to the south. Survivors fled to Malacca to establish the Malacca Sultanate.

events.title: Johor Sultanate Rule
events.description: Singapore became part of the Johor Sultanate, an insignificant fishing village called 'Temasek.' Occasionally frequented by Malay pirates.

events.title: Raffles Lands in Singapore
events.description: Sir Stamford Raffles, a British East India Company official, landed at the mouth of the Singapore River. Recognizing Singapore's strategic location, he decided to establish a British trading post there.

events.title: British Trading Post Established
events.description: Raffles signed a treaty with the Sultan of Johor and Temenggong, allowing Britain to establish a trading post in Singapore. Singapore became a free port and developed rapidly.

events.title: Raffles' City Planning
events.description: Raffles developed Singapore's city plan, segregating different ethnic groups (Chinese, Malay, Indian, European). This layout influences Singapore to this day.

events.title: Straits Settlements Formed
events.description: Singapore merged with Penang and Malacca to form the Straits Settlements, administered by British India. Singapore became a regional trading center.

events.title: Capital of Straits Settlements
events.description: Singapore replaced Penang as capital of the Straits Settlements. With its superior geographical location, Singapore rapidly developed into Southeast Asia's most important port.

events.title: British Crown Colony
events.description: The Straits Settlements transferred from British India to direct control by the British Colonial Office. Singapore's status was further elevated.

events.title: Mass Chinese Immigration
events.description: Large numbers of Chinese from Fujian and Guangdong migrated to Singapore for trade and labor. Chinese gradually became Singapore's largest ethnic group, bringing Chinese culture and dialects.

events.title: Raffles Institution Founded
events.description: Raffles Institution was established, becoming one of Singapore's most prestigious schools, educating many of Singapore's leaders.

events.title: Chinese Revolution and Singapore Chinese
events.description: Sun Yat-sen visited Singapore multiple times, receiving support from overseas Chinese. Many Singapore Chinese funded China's Xinhai Revolution.

events.title: Singapore Naval Base Construction
events.description: Britain began constructing the Singapore Naval Base, dubbed the 'Gibraltar of the East.' Completed in 1938, it was considered Southeast Asia's most powerful military fortress.

events.title: Fall of Singapore
events.description: Japanese forces captured Singapore from the Malay Peninsula in just one week. British forces surrendered, with about 80,000 British troops becoming prisoners of war. Churchill called it the 'worst disaster' in British military history.

events.title: Japanese Occupation (Syonan-to)
events.description: Japan renamed Singapore 'Syonan-to,' imposing brutal rule. Chinese faced mass killings (Sook Ching operation), with tens of thousands killed.

events.title: British Reoccupation
events.description: After Japan's surrender, British forces reoccupied Singapore. But Singaporeans' confidence in British protection was shattered, awakening nationalist consciousness.

events.title: Malayan Emergency
events.description: The Malayan Communist Party launched armed struggle, with Britain declaring a state of emergency. Singapore was also affected, with Britain intensifying Communist suppression.

events.title: People's Action Party Founded
events.description: Lee Kuan Yew and others founded the People's Action Party (PAP). Initially a left-wing coalition, PAP later became center-left, ruling Singapore to this day.

events.title: First Partial Self-Government Election
events.description: Singapore held its first Legislative Assembly election, implementing partial self-government. The Labour Front won, with David Marshall becoming the first Chief Minister.

events.title: Self-Governing State
events.description: Singapore became a British self-governing state with internal autonomy, while Britain retained defense and foreign affairs. PAP won elections, with Lee Kuan Yew becoming the first Prime Minister.

events.title: PAP Split
events.description: Left-wing forces within PAP split off to form the Barisan Sosialis (Socialist Front). Lee Kuan Yew turned to promoting Singapore's merger with Malaysia.

events.title: Joins Malaysia Federation
events.description: Singapore merged with Malaya, Sabah, and Sarawak to form the Federation of Malaysia. But Singapore quickly developed conflicts with the federal government.

events.title: Racial Riots
events.description: Racial riots erupted between Malays and Chinese in Singapore, causing casualties. Racial issues intensified tensions between Singapore and Malaysia's federal government.

events.title: Singapore Independence
events.description: Due to political and racial conflicts, Malaysia expelled Singapore from the federation. Singapore was forced into independence, becoming a sovereign nation. Lee Kuan Yew wept while announcing independence, concerned about the small nation's survival. August 9 became Singapore's National Day.

events.title: Early Nation-Building Challenges
events.description: Newly independent Singapore faced enormous challenges: no natural resources, small territory, high unemployment, housing shortage, racial tensions. Government began comprehensive development plans.

events.title: National Service System
events.description: Singapore implemented compulsory National Service, requiring all adult males to serve 2 years. This was crucial for the small nation's defense.

events.title: Singapore Dollar Independence
events.description: Singapore withdrew from the common currency zone with Malaysia and Brunei, issuing its own Singapore dollar. This was an important step toward economic independence.

events.title: Jurong Industrial Estate
events.description: Government vigorously developed Jurong Industrial Estate, attracting foreign investment. Singapore transitioned from entrepôt trade to manufacturing, accelerating industrialization.

events.title: British Military Withdrawal
events.description: Britain withdrew troops from Singapore, ending its military presence. Singapore had to rely entirely on its own defense forces.

events.title: Speak Mandarin Campaign
events.description: Government launched 'Speak Mandarin Campaign,' encouraging Chinese to speak Mandarin and stopping media use of dialects (Hokkien, Cantonese, etc.). This controversial policy was seen as promoting ethnic unity.

events.title: First MRT Line Begins
events.description: Singapore began constructing Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) system, with first line opening in 1987. MRT became the backbone of Singapore's public transport.

events.title: Singapore Airlines Rise
events.description: Singapore Airlines became a world-leading airline, with Changi Airport becoming Asia's major aviation hub. Aviation became a pillar of Singapore's economy.

events.title: Lee Kuan Yew Steps Down as PM
events.description: Lee Kuan Yew resigned as Prime Minister (though retaining Senior Minister status), with Goh Chok Tong taking over. Lee Kuan Yew ruled Singapore for 31 years, transforming it from a Third World to First World nation.

events.title: Asian Financial Crisis
events.description: The Asian Financial Crisis hit Singapore, causing economic recession. But with its sound financial system and foreign exchange reserves, Singapore was less affected and recovered quickly.

events.title: SARS Outbreak
events.description: The SARS outbreak struck Singapore, killing 33 people. Government responded swiftly, successfully controlling the outbreak and demonstrating crisis management capabilities.

events.title: Lee Hsien Loong Becomes PM
events.description: Lee Kuan Yew's eldest son Lee Hsien Loong became Prime Minister. Critics called this a 'family dynasty,' but supporters saw it as continuation of meritocratic governance.

events.title: First Integrated Resorts Open
events.description: Marina Bay Sands and Resorts World Sentosa, two integrated resorts (including casinos), opened, promoting tourism but also sparking social controversy.

events.title: Competitive Presidential Election
events.description: Presidential election saw rare intense competition, with Tony Tan winning by a narrow margin. This reflected subtle changes in Singapore's politics.

events.title: PAP Vote Share Declines
events.description: PAP's vote share in general elections fell to 60% (historic low), losing one GRC. This showed increased public dissatisfaction with the ruling party.

events.title: Little India Riot
events.description: Little India saw its first riot in 44 years, triggered by a traffic accident. Over 400 South Asian workers participated, highlighting foreign worker issues.

events.title: Death of Lee Kuan Yew
events.description: Singapore's founding father Lee Kuan Yew passed away at age 91. The nation mourned, with hundreds of thousands queuing to pay respects. Lee Kuan Yew is recognized as Singapore's greatest leader.

events.title: 50th Independence Anniversary
events.description: Singapore celebrated 50 years of independence (SG50). Singapore transformed from a poor island into a prosperous international financial center, with per capita GDP among the world's highest.

events.title: First Female President
events.description: Halimah Yacob was elected President (reserved election, limited to Malay candidates). She is Singapore's first female and Malay president.

events.title: Trump-Kim Summit in Singapore
events.description: Historic meeting between US President Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un was held in Singapore. This elevated Singapore's international status.

events.title: Lee's Brother Leaves PAP
events.description: Lee Hsien Loong's brother Lee Hsien Yang left PAP due to family property disputes and political differences, highlighting internal Lee family conflicts.

events.title: COVID-19 and Circuit Breaker
events.description: Singapore implemented 'Circuit Breaker' (similar to lockdown) to combat COVID-19. Foreign worker dormitories became outbreak hotspots. Singapore later adopted 'living with COVID' strategy.

events.title: PAP Vote Share Recovers
events.description: In elections held during the pandemic, PAP's vote share recovered to 61%. But opposition Workers' Party won 10 parliamentary seats, a historic high.

events.title: Repeal of Section 377A
events.description: Singapore repealed colonial-era Section 377A (criminalizing male homosexual conduct), but simultaneously amended the Constitution to define marriage as between one man and one woman.

events.title: Corruption Scandal Shakes Politics
events.description: Two ministers resigned over corruption scandal involving a property tycoon. This was Singapore's most serious political scandal in decades, damaging PAP's clean image.

events.title: Lawrence Wong Becomes PM
events.description: Lawrence Wong became Prime Minister, Singapore's fourth PM and the first born after the 1970s. He faces the challenge of leading Singapore into a new era.
